# Calibration: when 0.8 really means 80% {#sec-ch03}

If a model says 80%, does it really mean 80%? Nothing inside a model forces this to be true. It is true only if the model was built carefully and then checked. This chapter shows, in simple steps, how to check it and how to fix it. It is the most important habit in this book.

::: {.goals}
- Understand what *calibrated* means.
- Check a model's numbers with one simple chart.
- Know why a model's numbers go wrong, and how they are fixed.
:::

## What weather forecasters do well

In the 1970s, researchers in the United States compared weather forecasts with what actually happened. When forecasters said "30% chance of rain", it rained on about 30% of those days. When they said "70%", it rained on about 70% [@murphy1977]. Most people are not like this: we are usually too sure of ourselves.

![Two forecasters. For each thing they said ("30%", "70%" and so on), we count how often it actually happened. The careful forecaster sits on the diagonal: their 70% happens about 70% of the time. The overconfident one says 90% about things that happen only about 70% of the time.](/figures/ch04/forecasters.pdf){#fig-forecasters}

Good forecasters are not always right; nobody can be. They are good because their numbers mean what they say. This is called **calibration**.

::: {.keyidea}
**A model's "80%" must really mean 80%.** Take all the cases where it said 80%: about 80 out of 100 should turn out true. This is called being calibrated. If its 80% really means 50%, every decision based on it goes wrong.
:::

## How to check

@fig-forecasters is also the way to check any model. Take past cases where you already know the answer. Put them in groups by what the model said: 0–10%, 10–20%, and so on. In each group, count how often the event really happened. If the points lie on the diagonal line, the model's numbers can be trusted. If they lie below it, the model is too sure of itself.

To sum up the chart in one number, people use the **expected calibration error** (ECE): the average gap between what the model said and what really happened [@naeini2015]. In our example, the model's ECE is {{< num ch04 lr.ece f3 >}}, which means its numbers are off by less than one percentage point on average.

## Putting in order is not the same as correct numbers

A model's numbers can do two different jobs. Think of a teacher who ranks every student correctly, from first to last, but writes everyone's marks 30 points too high. The order is right; the marks are wrong.

- **Ranking**: does the model put the dangerous cases at the top of the list? This is measured by a score called **AUC**: 1 is perfect, and 0.5 is no better than tossing a coin.
- **Calibration**: are the numbers themselves correct?

A model can be good at ranking and still give wrong numbers. If you only want to know which alert to check first, ranking is enough. But if you use the numbers to decide, for example "close every alert below 10%", wrong numbers will mislead you.

::: {.keyidea}
**Putting cases in the right order is not enough; the numbers must also be right.** A model can put the most dangerous alerts at the top of the list and still say "40%" when the truth is "4%". To decide, you need both the right order and the right numbers.
:::

## Why the numbers go wrong, and how to fix them

Three things often spoil a model's numbers:

- **Training on a made-up 50/50 mix.** Attacks are rare, only {{< num ch04 base pct >}} of alerts in our example. So someone trains the model on equal numbers of attacks and normal alerts, "so it sees more attacks". The model then believes attacks are common: its average prediction becomes {{< num ch04 bal_mean_pred pct >}}. It is like a doctor who has worked only in a hospital ward and starts to think everyone is sick.
- **Large, over-trained models** become too sure of themselves and say "99%" too easily [@guo2017].
- **The world changes.** A sudden rise in attacks can make last month's correct numbers wrong today.

The good news: such a model usually does not need to be trained again. We keep aside some past cases the model has never seen, and learn a small correction on top of it. The two common corrections are **Platt scaling**, which moves all the numbers up or down and makes them more or less extreme [@platt1999], and **temperature scaling**, which only makes over-sure numbers less extreme. In our example, Platt scaling brought this 50/50 model's error down from {{< num ch04 balanced.ece f3 >}} to {{< num ch04 fixes.Platt.ece f3 >}}.

Finally, a model can be correct on average but wrong for one group. In our example, a model is correct for all alerts together, but for alerts from laptops it says {{< num ch04 by_source.EDR.pred pct1 >}} when the truth is {{< num ch04 by_source.EDR.actual pct1 >}}. The errors of different groups cancel out in the average, and real attacks on laptops get closed without anyone looking.

::: {.keyidea}
**A model that is right on average can still be wrong for one group.** It may be correct for all alerts together but wrong for laptop alerts, or for one language or one region. Check each group separately.
:::

::: {.breaks}
A model whose numbers were correct last month may not be correct today, because the world changes: new kinds of attacks, new software, new users. Also, correct numbers do not make every single answer right: if the model honestly says 70%, it will still be wrong about three times out of ten. So keep checking the model on recent cases, again and again.
:::

::: {.exercises}
1. Explain to a friend, without technical words, the difference between a model that ranks well and a model that is calibrated.
:::
